subject: Anthropology
title: Ethics in Fieldwork
description: A quick, practical guide to Ethics in Fieldwork.

hook.text: An anthropologist publishes secrets a community shared in trust. The village bans all researchers forever.

buildup.text: Fieldwork involves real people. Ethical guidelines protect their privacy, dignity, and right to refuse participation.

discovery.text: Informed consent means people must understand and agree to how their information will be used before sharing.

twist.text: Power imbalances are real. A Western researcher in a poor village holds enormous influence, even without meaning to.

climax.text: Ethics in anthropology means doing no harm — and recognizing that good intentions don't guarantee good outcomes.

punchline.text: Trust is the fieldworker's most fragile tool.

quiz.question: Why is informed consent essential in fieldwork?
options: People must understand and agree to how their information is used

details.summary: Ethical fieldwork requires informed consent, protecting confidentiality, avoiding harm, and ensuring research benefits the community studied. Anthropology's history includes ethical failures — complicity with colonialism, cold war intelligence gathering, and exploiting vulnerable populations.
details.whyItMatters: Ethical failures damaged communities and discredited anthropology. Modern ethical standards exist because past research caused real harm. Ethical fieldwork is not bureaucratic formality — it reflects the discipline's commitment to treating research.
takeaways: Ethical fieldwork requires consent, confidentiality, and harm avoidance
Anthropology's history includes complicity with colonialism and exploitation
Modern standards reflect commitments to treating people as partners

faq.question: What are the main ethical principles in anthropological research?
faq.answer: The American Anthropological Association's ethics code prioritizes: do no harm, obtain informed consent, protect confidentiality, make research accessible to communities, and be transparent about funding and intentions. Researchers must consider long-term consequences for the people they study.

faq.question: How has anthropology addressed its colonial past?
faq.answer: Through reflexive critique of the discipline's history, collaborative research methods that share authority with communities, indigenous anthropologists reclaiming their own narratives, and decolonization movements within professional organizations. Progress is real but incomplete.
